body.en: Summarise data with measures of centre and spread, and read trends from tables and plots.
The mean is the average, the median the middle value, the mode the most frequent, and the range the spread. A line of best fit models a linear trend in a scatter plot.

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Statistics & Data Analysis

body.en: Conditional Probability, Bayes' Theorem & Robust Summary Statistics: For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B) > 0\), conditional probability restricts the sample space to \(B\): \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\). In descriptive statistics, the median and interquartile range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)) are resistant to extreme outliers, whereas the mean \(\bar{x}\) and standard deviation \(s\) are pulled strongly in the direction of skewness.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Statistics & Data Analysis)

body.en:
Why Bayes' Theorem & Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion Work: Any event \(B\) can be partitioned into disjoint intersections \(B = (B \cap A) \cup (B \cap A')\). By additivity of mutually exclusive events and the multiplication rule \(P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)\):

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A')P(A')} \]

Similarly, in counting \(|A \cup B|\), summing \(|A| + |B|\) counts every element in \(A \cap B\) twice; subtracting \(|A \cap B|\) once restores exact cardinality: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).

Find the median and interquartile range (IQR) for the ordered dataset:

\[ 4,\ 7,\ 10,\ 14,\ 18,\ 22,\ 25. \]

The dataset has \( n = 7 \) values. The median is the 4th value: \( \text{Median} = 14 \).

Lower half: \( 4, 7, 10 \implies Q_1 = 7 \).

Upper half: \( 18, 22, 25 \implies Q_3 = 22 \).

The interquartile range is \( \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 22 - 7 = 15 \).

label.en: Common Pitfall — Mean vs. Median with Outliers

body.en: A high-frequency question on standardized math exams tests how adding extreme values alters summary statistics: Mean and range are sensitive to outliers and will shift substantially. Median and IQR are resistant — their values change very little (or not at all) when extreme outliers are added. In right-skewed data, \( \text{mean} > \text{median} \); in left-skewed data, \( \text{mean} < \text{median} \).

label.en: Worked Example \(C\) — Statistics & Data Analysis (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): A two-way table of \( N = 105 \) observations on study hall records cell counts \( B_1 = 12 \) for (Day, Library) and \( D_2 = 34 \) for (Evening, Commons). Determine the diagonal sum \( a = B_1 + D_2 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Summing the two frequencies gives \( 12 + 34 = 46 \).

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Statistics & Data Analysis (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): A two-way table of \( N = 107 \) observations on device preference records cell counts \( B_1 = 14 \) for (STEM, Tablet) and \( D_2 = 46 \) for (Arts, Laptop). Determine the diagonal sum \( a = B_1 + D_2 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Summing the two frequencies gives \( 14 + 46 = 60 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Statistics & Data Analysis)

rows.en: Using \(P(A \cap B) = 0\) when told \(A\) and \(B\) are independent
Confuses disjoint (mutually exclusive) events with statistically independent events.
For independent events, multiply probabilities: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)\).
Dividing by the grand total \(N\) when computing \(P(A \mid B)\) from a table
Computes the joint probability \(P(A \cap B)\) instead of conditioning on subset \(B\).
Restrict the denominator strictly to the row/column total of the given condition \(B\).
Using permutations \({}^nP_r\) when selecting a committee with no distinct roles
Overcounts every group of size \(r\) by \(r!\) internal orderings.

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Statistics & Data Analysis

body.en: Exam Strategy (Honors Algebra 1 & Foundations): Whenever a probability problem involves "at least one" success across multiple trials, immediately use the Complement Rule: \(P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})\). It turns a multi-case sum into a single calculation.

question.en: A distribution of test scores has first quartile \( Q_1 = 58 \) and third quartile \( Q_3 = 82 \). Using the standard \( 1.5 \times \text{IQR} \) rule, what is the lowest score that would NOT be considered an outlier?

solution.en:
First compute the interquartile range (IQR):

\[ \text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1 = 82 - 58 = 24. \]

Calculate the lower fence below which values are classified as low outliers:

\[ \text{Lower Fence} = Q_1 - 1.5(\text{IQR}) = 58 - 1.5(24) = 58 - 36 = 22. \]

Any score at or above \( 22 \) is not a low outlier. The lowest non-outlier score is \( 22 \).

question.en: A set of five exam scores has a mean of 84. Four of the scores are 78, 86, 92, and 80. Find the 5th score, and find the new mean if the lowest score is removed.

solution.en:
Total sum of the 5 scores = \(5 \times 84 = 420\).

Sum of the 4 known scores = \(78 + 86 + 92 + 80 = 336\).

5th score = \(420 - 336 = 84\).

Removing the lowest score (78) leaves four scores: 80, 84, 86, 92.

New sum = \(420 - 78 = 342\). New mean = \(342 / 4 = 85.5\) (an increase of 1.5 points).
